# Introduction
Thousands of blazes that have erupted in 2026 can be acrued to human activity, whether intentionally or accidental. A common reason is to clear land. Using fire is an inexpensive and fast way to prepare the ground for agriculture and plantations. The fires are also used to dispose of waste, especially in places with non-existent rubbish collection. Many fire hot spots also overlap with peatlands which are naturally wet ecosystems that become highly flammable when drained for plantation. With an exceptionally powerful El Nino this year, the fires can grow out of control rapidly, especially during prolonged dry spells. This has resulted in hazardous smoke spreading across the region. The smoke was then carried northwards by winds from the south, affecting neighbouring countries including Singapore. Transboundary haze pose significant environmental and public health threats to the region. With the haze-belching fires in Kalimantan and Sumatra driving Pollutant Standards Index (PSI) levels up, monitoring and predicting the magnitude of pollutants in the air across Singapore is critical for public health advisories (Rayda, 2026) (Mungcal et al., 2026). This project aims to accurately forecast regional air quality pollution levels across Singapore by leveraging on temporal dependencies and cross-station spatial patterns. By providing the framework, it would help deliver insights on the public health advisories such as outdoor activity restrictions, which ultimately mitigates acute respiratory and cardiovascular health risks. 
## Literature Review 
Traditional air quality forecasting approaches such as Multiple Linear Regression mainly rely on linear assumptions and have long served as standard baseline for air quality (Abdullah et al., 2020). Conversely, Machine Learning techniques account for non-linear relationships and time-lagged variables. Machine Leaning modeling frameworks such as Random Forest (RF), Artificial Neural Network (ANN) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have started to emerge as a way to effectively predict air quality (Palanichamy et al., 2022). Thus, this project investigates several machine learning algorithms for forecasting haze levels in Singapore, ultimately providing relevant information to responsible parties which allows them to mitigate and plan precautionary measures.

# Methodologies 
## Elastic Net Regression (Baseline Regularized Model)
## Random Forest
Linear models such as the elastic net cannot capture threshold effects, for example wind speed needing to exceed a critical value before smoke plumes reach Singapore. To account for such non-linear atmospheric interactions, we train a Random Forest (Breiman, 2001) of 500 trees to forecast the PSI level in the west region at two horizons: $t+1$ hour (immediate) and $t+6$ hours (extended). Predictors at time $t$ comprise the PSI of all five regions at lags 0 to 5 hours, wind vector components ($u$, $w$) and mean wind speed, and daily fire radiative power and hotspot counts for Sumatra and Kalimantan, together with the Sumatra smoke-transport interaction term. The number of variables tried at each split (`mtry`) is selected by minimising the out-of-bag (OOB) mean squared error. The data are split by time (training: 1 August to 10 October 2019; testing: 11 to 31 October 2019) to avoid leaking future observations into training. As this split is deterministic, all models in the group are evaluated on the same test set. Variable importance is measured by permutation: the percentage increase in OOB MSE when a predictor's values are randomly shuffled. Predictors are grouped into local (west) lags, other-region lags, wind, and fire/smoke transport to assess whether local persistence or upstream burning dominates as the horizon lengthens. Forecasts are compared against the elastic net and a persistence benchmark (forecast = current west PSI) using RMSE, MAE and $R^2$.

## VARX Spatio-Temporal Model
To capture spatial inter-dependencies across Singapore’s five geographic zones simultaneously, we fit a Vector Autoregressive Exogenous (VARX) model. Unlike single-region regressors that forecast zones in isolation, the VARX framework models the five regional air quality series as an interconnected endogenous vector system, $\mathbf{Y}_t = [\text{North}_t, \text{South}_t, \text{East}_t, \text{West}_t, \text{Central}_t]^T$, driven by exogenous wind vectors and Indonesian smoke advection inputs, $\mathbf{X}_t$. The exogenous feature matrix $\mathbf{X}_t$ comprises wind velocity components ($u$, $w$), daily fire radiative power in Sumatra, and the Sumatra smoke-transport interaction term. Stationarity across all five series in $\mathbf{Y}_{\text{train}}$ was verified using Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) tests. Optimal lag length $p$ for the endogenous components was selected via `VARselect()` by minimizing the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) up to a maximum lag of 10 hours. Directional transmission across regional pairs under prevailing monsoonal winds was evaluated using pairwise Granger causality tests (`causality()`). To trace how incoming smoke fronts physically diffuse across the island network, orthogonalized Impulse Response Functions (IRFs) were simulated over a 24-hour horizon following a 1-unit shock at entry regions (South and West). Finally, multi-step out-of-sample forecasts were generated on the test set (11 to 31 October 2019) using `predict()` with exogenous test inputs $\mathbf{X}_{\text{test}}$, and evaluated on the West region using RMSE, MAE, and $R^2$.

# Results
## Model Evaluation and Comparison 
### Forecast Accuracy at $t+1$ and $t+6$ Hours
The table below compares the Random Forest against the elastic net and a persistence benchmark (forecast = current west PSI) on the test set (11 to 31 October 2019). For a like-for-like comparison, the elastic net was refitted on the same time-based split and feature set, so its figures here may differ from the Phase 2 baseline, which uses lagged PSI only.

| Horizon | Model | RMSE | MAE | $R^2$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $t+1$ hr | Persistence | 6.45 | 4.90 | 0.462 |
| $t+1$ hr | Elastic Net | 5.79 | 4.62 | 0.493 |
| $t+1$ hr | Random Forest | 6.23 | 5.02 | 0.443 |
| $t+6$ hr | Persistence | 9.18 | 7.28 | 0.122 |
| $t+6$ hr | Elastic Net | 7.87 | 6.15 | 0.152 |
| $t+6$ hr | Random Forest | 13.30 | 9.87 | 0.030 |

At the $t+1$ hr horizon, the elastic net achieved the lowest error (RMSE 5.79). The Random Forest (RMSE 6.23) offered only a small improvement over the persistence benchmark (RMSE 6.45) and did not beat the linear baseline, and its MAE (5.02) was slightly worse than persistence (4.90). All three models explained less than half of the variance ($R^2 \le 0.49$).

Forecast accuracy deteriorated for every model at $t+6$ hr. The elastic net remained the best model (RMSE 7.87, $R^2$ 0.15), while the Random Forest performed worst (RMSE 13.30, $R^2$ 0.03), doing worse than the persistence benchmark. Figure 1 shows why: the Random Forest tracks actual PSI reasonably well at $t+1$ hr, but at $t+6$ hr it produces large spurious spikes of about 50 PSI in mid and late October (around 13 to 16 October and 24 to 26 October), when observed PSI stayed near 20.

![Random Forest forecasts vs actual west PSI on the test period](forecast_plot.png)

### Permutation Variable Importance
Permutation importance was computed for each horizon as the percentage increase in MSE when a predictor is shuffled. To assess whether local persistence or upstream drivers dominate, predictors were grouped into local (west) lags, other-region lags, wind, and fire/smoke transport (see table below, Figure 2). Because the groups contain different numbers of variables, the table also reports the average importance per variable.

| Horizon | Group | Share of total importance | Avg. importance per variable |
|---|---|---|---|
| $t+1$ hr | Local (west) lags | 21.1% | 10.8 |
| $t+1$ hr | Other-region lags | 61.7% | 7.9 |
| $t+1$ hr | Wind | 5.5% | 5.6 |
| $t+1$ hr | Fire / smoke transport | 11.8% | 7.3 |
| $t+6$ hr | Local (west) lags | 13.6% | 8.9 |
| $t+6$ hr | Other-region lags | 51.2% | 8.3 |
| $t+6$ hr | Wind | 10.4% | 13.6 |
| $t+6$ hr | Fire / smoke transport | 24.8% | 19.4 |

![Share of permutation importance by predictor group](group_plot.png)

At $t+1$ hr, lagged PSI readings account for most of the importance (local lags 21.1% and other-region lags 61.7%), and local lags have the highest importance per variable. This indicates that short-term forecasts are driven mainly by recent PSI persistence and cross-station spatial patterns. At $t+6$ hr, the share of local lags falls to 13.6%, while the shares of fire/smoke transport (11.8% to 24.8%) and wind (5.5% to 10.4%) roughly double, and each fire variable becomes more than twice as important as a typical lag variable.

![Permutation importance of the top 15 predictors](importance_plot.png)

Figure 3 shows the top 15 predictors at each horizon. At $t+1$ hr, the most important variables are the most recent PSI readings across all regions (e.g. `Lag_west_0`, `Lag_north_0`, `Lag_central_0`), with fire variables ranking lower. At $t+6$ hr the ranking changes: Sumatra and Kalimantan fire radiative power (`daily_frp_Sumatra`, `daily_frp_Kalimantan`), the hotspot counts, the smoke-transport term, and the north-south wind component (`wind_w`) all enter the top eight, together with only two PSI lags (`Lag_east_0`, `Lag_west_1`). Upstream burning and southerly wind transport therefore become the dominant signals as the horizon lengthens, while local persistence fades.

However, higher importance does not imply better forecasts. The $t+6$ hr Random Forest, which relies most on the fire variables, generalised worst to the October test period. A possible reason is that the fire variables are daily values that are constant within each day, so the forest may have used them to memorise the training days rather than learn a relationship that holds in October. Future work could use lagged or smoothed fire features and time-series cross-validation to reduce this.

## VARX Spatio-Temporal Model

### Optimal Lag Selection & Granger Causality
ADF tests confirmed stationarity across all five regional training series ($p < 0.01$). Model lag selection via `VARselect()` identified $p = 3$ hours as optimal under AIC, indicating that a 3-hour lookback window provides maximum predictive memory for the joint regional system. Pairwise Granger causality tests confirmed statistically significant directional transmission ($p < 0.001$) across all regional pairs. Given Singapore's compact geographic footprint, air masses create high spatial autocorrelation across the island, confirming that past observations in entry zones contain unique predictive information for adjacent central and northern zones.

### Spatial Diffusion Profiles (Impulse Response Functions)
Impulse Response Functions (IRFs) simulated over a 24-hour horizon map the physical transmission delays across Singapore following a shock at key entry points (Figure 1 and Figure 2).

| Entry Region | Peak Response Time (Other Regions) | Relative Peak Magnitude | Primary Physical Behavior |
|---|---|---|---|
| **South** | 2 to 3 hours post-shock | High ($\sim 2.0 - 2.5\ \mu\text{g/m}^3$) | Fast advection northward along the central corridor under prevailing winds. |
| **West** | 4 to 6 hours post-shock | Moderate ($\sim 0.5 - 1.0\ \mu\text{g/m}^3$) | Slower cross-island drift with greater spatial dissipation from the western edge. |

![Island-Wide PM2.5 Response to South Shock](irf_south.png)

![Island-Wide PM2.5 Response to West Shock](irf_west.png)

A shock originating in the South region causes an immediate own-region spike at $t=0$ ($\sim 6.5\ \mu\text{g/m}^3$) and reaches peak impact in neighboring regions 2 to 3 hours post-shock. Conversely, a shock originating in the West region takes 4 to 6 hours to peak in eastern and northern zones with lower overall magnitude, reflecting longer travel distance across land and greater spatial dissipation.

### Out-of-Sample Forecast Accuracy (West Region)
The table below compares the dynamic multi-step VARX forecast against the Elastic Net baseline, Random Forest, and Persistence benchmark on the test set (11 to 31 October 2019).

| Horizon / Framework | Model | RMSE | MAE | $R^2$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $t+1$ hr | Persistence | 6.45 | 4.90 | 0.462 |
| $t+1$ hr | Elastic Net | 5.79 | 4.62 | 0.493 |
| $t+1$ hr | Random Forest | 6.23 | 5.02 | 0.443 |
| $t+6$ hr | Persistence | 9.18 | 7.28 | 0.122 |
| $t+6$ hr | Elastic Net | 7.87 | 6.15 | 0.152 |
| $t+6$ hr | Random Forest | 13.30 | 9.87 | 0.030 |
| Dynamic (504-Step Test) | VARX System | 11.17 | 8.97 | 0.031 |

Across the 504-step holdout test set, the VARX model achieved an RMSE of 11.17 $\mu\text{g/m}^3$, an MAE of 8.97 $\mu\text{g/m}^3$, and an $R^2$ of 0.031. Over an extended 21-day un-updated forecast horizon, VARX performs worse than 1-step-ahead models ($t+1$ hr Elastic Net RMSE 5.79), but outperforms the extended 6-step-ahead Random Forest ($t+6$ hr RMSE 13.30, $R^2$ 0.030).

![VARX Out-of-Sample PM2.5 Forecast (West Region)](varx_eval_plot.png)

As shown in Figure 3, the VARX forecast (red dashed line) generates a smoothed trajectory that successfully captures the macro-level trend and low-frequency accumulation cycles over the 3-week test period, correctly identifying major haze build-ups around mid-October (14–16 Oct) and late October (24–25 Oct). Because the linear system minimizes overall mean squared error, it acts as a low-pass filter that dampens sharp hourly volatility and underpredicts extreme peaks. During sudden mid-month surges, autoregressive lags introduce a minor phase delay, whereas toward late October, updated wind vector changes ($\mathbf{X}_t$) act as leading indicators, pulling predictions downward slightly before ground-level sensors register concentration drops.
